title: Real-Life Graphs
content:
# Real-Life Graphs

> **Tier:** Foundation and Higher

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Interpret and draw distance-time graphs
- Use and interpret conversion graphs
- Calculate and interpret gradients in real-life contexts
- Read values from real-life graphs and explain what they represent
- Understand the difference between linear and non-linear real-life graphs

## Introduction

Graphs are used every day to represent real-world situations: tracking a journey on a distance-time graph, converting between currencies, monitoring temperature changes, or comparing costs. Being able to read, draw, and interpret these graphs is one of the most practical mathematical skills you will learn.

---

## Key Concepts

### Distance-Time Graphs

**A distance-time graph** shows how the distance from a starting point changes over time.

- **The horizontal axis** represents time.
- **The vertical axis** represents distance from the starting point.
- **A horizontal line** means the object is stationary (not moving).
- **A straight line going up** means the object is moving at a constant speed.
- **A steeper line** means a faster speed.
- **A line going down** means the object is returning to the starting point.

### Gradient = Speed

On a distance-time graph, the **gradient** (slope) represents the **speed**:

$$\text{Speed} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} = \text{Gradient of the line}$$

### Conversion Graphs

**A conversion graph** is a straight-line graph that converts between two units or quantities, such as:
- Miles and kilometres
- Pounds sterling and euros
- Celsius and Fahrenheit

To use a conversion graph, start at a value on one axis, draw across (or up) to the line, then read the corresponding value on the other axis.

### Interpreting the Gradient in Context

The gradient always represents a **rate of change**. The meaning depends on the context:

| Graph Type | Gradient Represents |
|------------|--------------------|
| Distance-time | Speed |
| Cost vs quantity | Price per item |
| Volume vs time | Flow rate |
| Currency conversion | Exchange rate |
| Depth vs time | Rate of filling/emptying |

---

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: Reading a Distance-Time Graph

**Question:** A cyclist leaves home at 9:00 am. The distance-time graph shows their journey.
- From 9:00 to 10:00 they travel 15 km.
- From 10:00 to 10:30 they stop for a rest.
- From 10:30 to 11:30 they travel a further 20 km.

Calculate the speed for each section.

**Solution:**

**Section 1 (9:00 to 10:00):**
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Speed} &= \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} \\
&= \frac{15 \text{ km}}{1 \text{ hour}} \\
&= 15 \text{ km/h}
\end{aligned}$$

**Section 2 (10:00 to 10:30):**
The cyclist is stationary, so the speed is $0$ km/h.

**Section 3 (10:30 to 11:30):**
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Speed} &= \frac{20 \text{ km}}{1 \text{ hour}} \\
&= 20 \text{ km/h}
\end{aligned}$$

The third section is steeper, confirming the cyclist was travelling faster.

---

### Example 2: Conversion Graph

**Question:** A conversion graph shows that 5 miles = 8 km. Use this to convert:
(a) 20 miles to km
(b) 40 km to miles

**Solution:**

The conversion rate is:
$$\frac{8 \text{ km}}{5 \text{ miles}} = 1.6 \text{ km per mile}$$

**(a)** $20 \text{ miles} = 20 \times 1.6 = 32$ km

**(b)** $40 \text{ km} = 40 \div 1.6 = 25$ miles

On a conversion graph, you would read across from 20 on the miles axis to the line, then down to the km axis to get 32.

---

### Example 3: Interpreting Gradient in Context

**Question:** A graph shows the cost of printing leaflets. At 100 leaflets the cost is £30, and at 300 leaflets the cost is £50. Find and interpret the gradient.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Gradient} &= \frac{\text{Change in cost}}{\text{Change in quantity}} \\
&= \frac{50 - 30}{300 - 100} \\
&= \frac{20}{200} \\
&= 0.10
\end{aligned}$$

**Interpretation:** Each additional leaflet costs **£0.10** (10p) to print.

Note: The graph does not pass through the origin, suggesting there is a **fixed cost** (setup charge) in addition to the per-leaflet cost.

---

### Example 4: Return Journey on a Distance-Time Graph

**Question:** A walker leaves home at 2:00 pm, walks 6 km in 1.5 hours, rests for 30 minutes, then walks back home in 1 hour. Calculate the speed of the return journey and the average speed for the whole trip.

**Solution:**

**Return journey speed:**
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Speed} &= \frac{6 \text{ km}}{1 \text{ hour}} \\
&= 6 \text{ km/h}
\end{aligned}$$

**Average speed for the whole trip:**
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Total distance} &= 6 + 6 = 12 \text{ km} \\
\text{Total time} &= 1.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 3 \text{ hours} \\
\text{Average speed} &= \frac{12}{3} = 4 \text{ km/h}
\end{aligned}$$

> **Key Insight:** Average speed uses **total distance** divided by **total time**, including rest stops.

---

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Forgetting to include rest time in average speed | Average speed uses total time for the whole journey | Total distance $\div$ total time (including stops) |
| Reading the wrong axis | Confusing which axis is distance and which is time | Always check axis labels carefully |
| Thinking a horizontal line means constant speed | A horizontal line means zero distance covered | Horizontal = stationary (speed = 0) |
| Confusing speed and distance | The gradient gives speed, not the height of the line | Height = distance from start; gradient = speed |
| Ignoring units | Mixing hours and minutes gives wrong speeds | Convert all times to the same unit before calculating |

---

## Practice Questions

### Foundation Level

1. A car travels 60 km in 2 hours at constant speed. What is the speed?

2. On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line represent?

3. A bus journey is shown on a distance-time graph. The bus travels 30 km in the first hour, stops for 15 minutes, then travels 15 km in 45 minutes. Calculate the speed for each moving section.

4. A conversion graph shows 10 euros = £8.50. Convert:
   - (a) 30 euros to pounds
   - (b) £34 to euros

5. A delivery company charges a fixed fee of £5 plus £2 per kg. Draw a graph and use it to find the cost of a 7 kg parcel.

6. A cyclist rides 24 km in 1.5 hours, rests for 30 minutes, then rides 16 km in 1 hour. Calculate the average speed for the entire journey.

### Higher Level

7. A graph of cost against number of units of electricity shows a gradient of 0.15. Interpret this value.

8. Two friends set off on a walk at the same time. Person A walks at 5 km/h. Person B walks at 3 km/h but had a 2 km head start. After how long does Person A catch up with Person B? Set up and solve using a distance-time graph approach.

9. A bath is filled at a constant rate for 5 minutes, then the tap is turned off for 3 minutes, then the plug is pulled and the bath empties in 8 minutes. Sketch a depth-time graph and calculate the rate of emptying if the maximum depth was 40 cm.

10. A currency conversion graph passes through the origin and the point $(100, 85)$. Find the gradient and explain what it represents.

11. A car journey has three stages: 40 km at 80 km/h, a 15-minute stop, then 30 km at 60 km/h. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.

12. Explain why a distance-time graph can never go below the horizontal axis.

---

## Answers

1. Speed $= \frac{60}{2} = 30$ km/h

2. The object is stationary (not moving).

3. First section: $\frac{30}{1} = 30$ km/h. Second section: $\frac{15}{0.75} = 20$ km/h.

4. (a) $30 \times 0.85 = £25.50$ (b) $34 \div 0.85 = 40$ euros

5. Cost $= 5 + 2(7) = £19$

6. Total distance $= 24 + 16 = 40$ km. Total time $= 1.5 + 0.5 + 1 = 3$ hours. Average speed $= \frac{40}{3} = 13.\overline{3}$ km/h $\approx 13.3$ km/h.

7. Each additional unit of electricity costs £0.15.

8. Person A: distance $= 5t$. Person B: distance $= 2 + 3t$. Setting equal: $5t = 2 + 3t$, so $2t = 2$, giving $t = 1$ hour.

9. Rate of emptying $= \frac{40}{8} = 5$ cm per minute. The graph rises linearly for 5 min, is flat for 3 min, then decreases linearly for 8 min back to 0.

10. Gradient $= \frac{85}{100} = 0.85$. This means £1 converts to 0.85 of the other currency (or for every 100 units of the foreign currency, you receive £85).

11. Time for stage 1: $\frac{40}{80} = 0.5$ h. Stop: $0.25$ h. Time for stage 3: $\frac{30}{60} = 0.5$ h. Total time $= 1.25$ h. Total distance $= 70$ km. Average speed $= \frac{70}{1.25} = 56$ km/h.

12. Distance from the starting point cannot be negative. The graph may come back down to zero (returning to the start), but not below.

---

## Exam Tips

- Always check the units on both axes before reading values.
- When calculating speed from a distance-time graph, make sure your time is in the correct units (convert minutes to hours if the distance is in km).
- If the question asks for average speed, use total distance and total time -- do not average the individual speeds.
- Show your gradient calculations clearly: write the change in $y$ over the change in $x$ with units.
- For conversion graphs, read values carefully by drawing lines across and down to the axes.

---

## Summary

- **Distance-time graphs**: gradient = speed; horizontal line = stationary; steeper = faster
- **Conversion graphs**: straight-line graphs used to convert between two quantities
- **Gradient** in context represents a **rate of change** (speed, cost per item, flow rate, etc.)
- **Average speed** = total distance $\div$ total time (including stops)
- Always check **units** and **axis labels** when reading real-life graphs
- A line returning to the horizontal axis means returning to the starting point
